blocks.md: This lesson follows **Fallacies and Pitfalls** in *Supervisory Intervention* (Vol IV).

blocks.source: Vol IV, Supervisory Intervention, § Fallacies and Pitfalls
blocks.md: Flipping a bit in an authority register does not complete a safe supervisory handover. A real-time physical AI system must preserve its dynamic stopping margin and protective enforcement functions throughout every stage of transfer. Furthermore, downstream imitation learning pipelines cannot treat intervention logs as unblemished expert recoveries without explicit causal filtering. When systems fail in deployment, the breakdown almost always traces back to one of four subtle architectural traps.

questions.q: The section **Fallacies and Pitfalls** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A takeover log is split into intervals by commit, blend-end, and stabilization timestamps, and only the stabilized human interval trains as demonstration.
Reconstruction needs a log that survives physical failure and records both sides of the causal boundary on synchronized clocks, because dispatched commands alone cannot prove delivered torque.

Fixing the current speed and solving the stopping inequality for the wait gives the latest fallback deadline, so a handover timeout is a function of state, and any configured ceiling is clipped to it.
Per channel, authority resolves every tick to exactly one state with the enforcer the sole actuator writer, and a four-phase request-acknowledge-commit-release handshake moves it.
